hints.junior: The user sees a decoy button, but the click actually lands on a real, nearly-invisible control stacked on top of it.
hints.mid: A browser delivers a click to whatever's topmost at that pixel — an attacker exploits that gap between what's visible and what's actually there.
hints.staff: This isn't a same-origin-policy problem — the attacker never reads any data, they misdirect a real, authenticated click the victim's own browser is already willing to send.

hints.junior: Check "Reveal hidden layer" to see what's really stacked over the decoy in each mode, then click it and watch what happens.
hints.mid: In the vulnerable mode, the topmost element receiving your click isn't the decoy you see — in the protected mode, there's nothing there to receive it at all.
hints.staff: This is simulated locally with no real cross-origin iframe, but the layering, opacity, and click-target mechanics mirror a real attacker's page exactly.

hints.junior: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' tells the browser only your own origin may embed this page — anyone else's frame just fails to load.
hints.mid: frame-ancestors accepts a real source list — specific origins, wildcarded subdomains, 'self', or 'none' — unlike X-Frame-Options' blunt DENY/SAMEORIGIN pair.
hints.staff: Send both headers together for defense in depth, and remember frame-ancestors doesn't fall back to default-src the way most other CSP directives do.

hints.junior: Even a maximally locked-down default-src 'none' policy still allows framing by anyone unless frame-ancestors is set explicitly.
hints.mid: SameSite cookies are a second, independent layer — they can stop authenticated cookies from riding along on a cross-site framed request in the first place.
hints.staff: Verify the header actually landed with a real cross-origin framing test — a common failure mode is setting it on the HTML document but missing an API or SSR edge case.

sections.junior: Today's case is about clickjacking, where a page gets embedded invisibly inside another site so a click meant for a decoy lands on a real, hidden control instead.
sections.mid: A browser sends a click to whatever element is topmost at that exact point on screen, whether or not a person can actually see it there.
sections.staff: This isn't about stealing data across origins. It's about misdirecting a real, logged-in click the victim's own browser is already willing to send.

sections.junior: Sending one response header tells the browser only your own site is allowed to embed this page in a frame, so nobody else's frame will even load.
sections.mid: This header is the modern replacement for an older one that only supported two blunt options, deny everyone or allow only the same origin.
sections.staff: It's worth sending both the old and new headers together, and remembering the new one doesn't inherit from a page's other content security policy rules.

sections.junior: Try revealing the hidden layer in both modes to see what's actually stacked over the button you can see.
sections.mid: Notice that in the protected mode, your click falls straight through to the harmless decoy, because there's nothing else there to catch it.
sections.staff: Everything here runs locally with plain DOM elements, no real iframe or cross-origin request involved, only the mechanics are faithful.

sections.junior: Send the frame-ancestors header so the browser refuses to load your page inside anyone else's frame in the first place.
sections.mid: It replaces the older X-Frame-Options header with a real list of allowed origins, and sending both together covers older clients too.
sections.staff: Remember it doesn't inherit from your other policy rules, pair it with SameSite cookies, and actually verify it landed on every route that matters.
